Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time. Code/dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/GeoWind2Plan/ . Demo: https://geowind2plan.com .

articles.title: Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination for Hospital Patient Flow Optimization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.37022v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Efficient patient flow coordination across autonomous hospital departments is critical for mitigating overcrowding and balancing resource utilization. While classical queueing theory, specifically open Baskett--Chandy--Muntz--Palacios (BCMP) networks, provides an interpretable mathematical topology for healthcare operations, analytical models rely on stationary assumptions and fixed routing matrices that degrade under state-dependent real-world dynamics. Conversely, centralized reinforcement learning approaches struggle to accommodate the decentralized structure of hospital governance, where individual clinical departments function with localized observations, heterogeneous resources, and divergent operational objectives. In this paper, we present a Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) framework titled \emph{Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination}, which embeds empirically calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors within a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Formulated as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under coupled resource constraints, our method enables autonomous departmental agents to cooperatively negotiate patient routing and dynamic service scaling. To mitigate environmental non-stationarity without inducing excessive communication overhead, agents exchange localized action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward structure. Empirical evaluations driven by real-world MIMIC-IV patient trajectories indicate that this cooperative multi-agent approach substantially reduces cumulative system delay compared to static Markovian approximations, heuristic dispatching, and independent multi-agent baselines, while maintaining clinical safety constraints.

articles.title: ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.37311v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive web platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a recommendation-agent framework, termed ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item-page screenshots and uses an OCR tool to produce structured textual evidence for the reasoning backbone. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential update strategy that maintains a bounded textual memory while processing histories longer than the backbone context window; with fixed chunk and memory budgets, the number of update calls grows linearly with history length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To train the dynamic memory updater, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant whose reward combines recommendation-specific information with final-task metrics. Experiments on three Amazon-derived datasets and a controlled post-retrieval protocol show an average relative improvement of 7.58% over the strongest reported baseline across searching, ranking, and judging tasks.

articles.title: Alleviating Hallucination in Reasoning Tasks with Training-Free Uncertainty-Guided Steering
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38962v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent work on hallucination detection in large language models has shown that, for a fixed pre-trained model and reasoning task, it is possible to estimate the model's confidence in the correctness of its outputs. Such uncertainty estimates have primarily been used to improve truthfulness by detecting or filtering confabulations. In this work, we ask whether these signals can instead be used more proactively to directly improve the accuracy of model-generated answers. We propose USteer, a simple, training-free steering mechanism that adjusts a model's layer-wise activations during inference using the gradient of a confidence measure with respect to the activations. This procedure nudges generation toward outputs with lower uncertainty at inference time, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional supervision. We show that this approach consistently reduces hallucination across a range of reasoning tasks, demonstrating that confidence signals can be leveraged not only for detection, but also for effective inference-time control of model behavior.

articles.title: What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.01002v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

articles.title: LUMOS: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.02902v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Current analyses of LLMs' parametric knowledge are largely output-centric, drawing conclusions about what a model knows without verifying what it was actually trained on. This leaves fundamental questions, such as whether a correct response reflects genuine generalization or rote memorization, grounded in speculation rather than evidence. To resolve these ambiguities, we introduce LUMOS, a diagnostic framework that traces knowledge across training-data exposure, internal representations, and behavioral outputs, leveraging OLMo 2 with its fully transparent training corpus. By grounding analysis in verified exposure, we reveal that models internally encode rare facts with high separability (84%) yet fail to express them behaviorally (54%), though this retrieval gap narrows with scale. Furthermore, when models are asked to self-reflect on their own answers, they perform reliably on trained content (83%) but drop to random-baseline levels (49%) on unseen content. This collapse persists even under chain-of-thought prompting, which inflates confidence signals rather than improving calibration. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that incorporating the training-data axis into LLM evaluation transforms speculative diagnoses into verifiable claims, and we advocate that this axis should be a standard component of knowledge assessment in LLMs.

articles.title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.04510v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics, chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations per sample. We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. All existing acceleration families fail on this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry, inducing mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache, the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Exploiting this structure, we prove that the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp safe-caching boundary: caching before it incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a strictly positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion, a gap that persists up to the boundary. We further prove that deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides within the safe phase, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires no calibration data, along with zero training overhead.

articles.title: From Dialogue to Diagnostic Hypotheses: Evaluating LLM Agents for Psychiatric Assessment
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.07473v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Although LLMs show promising diagnostic reasoning on supplied clinical evidence, their ability to elicit such evidence through free-form psychiatric interviews remains less understood. We evaluate interview quality and diagnostic hypotheses using simulated patients and human participants. For controlled simulation, we introduce PsyCPG, transforming clinical cases into structured patient profiles. On 30 paired cases, experts rate PsyCPG simulations higher in quality than raw-case role-play (4.50 versus 3.83/5). We introduce PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework: its interviewer agent uses a notepad tool, expert-written skills, and ICD-11 reference tools to guide interviews; its diagnostic agent analyzes the transcript and produces a report for expert review, ranking differential diagnoses with supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence. Across four models and 53 development cases, PsyCIDRA achieves higher observed diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, exact-code rank-1 accuracy reaches 60.5% versus 51.9%. We conduct 101 interviews with human participants; two psychologists, blinded to interview condition and model reports, independently assess interview quality and transcript-supported hypotheses. In separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with experts on whether to issue a hypothesis in 79.6% of cases versus 65.4% for direct prompting. This study provides an empirical basis for understanding and evaluating LLM agents in free-form psychiatric interviewing.

articles.title: AssemState: Manual and Physical-State-Guided Reasoning for Zero-shot Furniture Assembly
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.08446v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding, but precise 3D spatial reasoning integrated with physical environment remains difficult. Furniture assembly requires not only recovering step-level operations from diagrammatic manuals, but also translating semantic attachment relations into 6D pose updates that enable parts to physically interact with the environment and previously assembled components. To study this problem, we propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework for manual and physical-state-guided furniture assembly. It firstly employs anchor-guided boundary assembly states to decompose manual pages into single-part operations and recover an assembly-tree. Then, it uses iterative after-state feedback refinement to guide successive (SE(3)) updates and corrections, and validates their physical plausibility through simulation-based release tests. Experiments show that compared with the strongest prior baseline, AssemState improves F1 from 38.58\% to 62.80\% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24\% to 53.92\% for assembly-tree recovery. On 243 independently evaluated part-level operations, our proposed iterative refinement improves judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3\% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. However, visually plausible candidate poses may still suffer from collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment. These results show that AssemState improves operation-structure recovery and selected local pose metrics, while MLLMs remain limited for spatial relationship reasoning.

articles.title: Self-Supervised Keyframe Discovery for Horizon-Invariant Behavior Cloning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.10857v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) in non-Markovian environments is a challenging problem because policies have to reason over contextual information over long horizons. Existing policy architectures rely on recurrent or attention-based mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies. However, recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse and gradient instability under backpropagation through time while attention-based models are fundamentally limited by context length. To address these issues, we propose Keyframe Mnemonics, a novel self-supervised method that $\textit{discovers}$ a set of information-critical observations ($\textit{mnemonics}$) by learning an objective from randomly sampled past observations and using it as a reward for keyframe selection. We then train a BC policy that conditions on the discovered keyframes to model the action distribution. Under the simplicity bias assumption, our formulation provides context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon, while maintaining a small set of decision-relevant keyframes in the policy's working memory. We evaluate our method on synthetic memory domains, where mnemonic-conditioned BC policies achieve $100$% success rates (SR) and generalize to horizons orders of magnitude beyond training without performance degradation. Moreover, we evaluate on a memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark, achieving a $13.9$% average absolute SR improvement over the strongest baseline across $23$ tasks. Finally, we demonstrate generalization with $80$% SR at $20\times$ longer time horizons on a real robot. Code and videos available at https://keyframe-mnemonics.github.io.

articles.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.14381v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark that separates the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: natural-language scenarios describe the system, while a hidden causal model defines the data, the effect of every intervention, and the oracle answers. In ACED-Repair, agents diagnose a failing production system: within 15 experiments they must decide which controls to test, read confounded and filtered data, and recommend a fix, which we re-simulate on a hidden true objective. In ACED-Query, agents answer causal questions and make constrained causal decisions in worlds backed by categorical probabilistic graphical models. Acceptance on ACED-Repair ranges from 43% to 0% across 12 LLMs, while strong agents approach ceiling on ACED-Query's qualification questions. Tracing every experiment shows where investigations stop: most open-weight models test a true lever on its own in fewer than half of the worlds, the strongest models test the right levers but often miss the working dose or combination, and agents that do run a working fix almost always recommend it. No model reliably repairs systems with two independent causes or systems that need a subgroup-specific policy. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for choosing experiments, keeping track of evidence, and composing interventions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/ACED-Bench.

articles.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.16776v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. It then projects that document into a runtime scaffold, machine-readable contracts, and deterministic tests. Eight specialized agents next carry out production: scenes are implemented serially, assets are produced in parallel, and one reduced manifest joins the two branches into a single build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. We evaluate finished games separately, through their rendered interfaces alone, over prompt-matched tasks run under a common protocol. GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline. In a side-by-side human study, raters also score GCA's games higher on every dimension and prefer them overall.

articles.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Decision Rules in an Agent-Based Agro-Ecological Model
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.22420v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agent-based models are well-suited for modelling agro-ecological systems for decision-making, yet turning their simulations into actionable insight requires identifying which decisions actually drive the behaviours. In such a context, sensitivity analysis stumbles upon a structural feature of many complex systems: the parameters are not a flat vector but a decision tree in which many parameters appear only when a higher-level choice activates them. Classical global sensitivity analysis presupposes independent inputs over a fixed Cartesian product and is ill-posed on such a branched space and biased by construction. We instead treat the structure of the decisions as a first-class modelling object. Using advanced surrogate modelling techniques, we encode the crop-management itinerary of the high-resolution agro-ecological modelling platform MAELIA as a hierarchical design space featuring both categorical and numerical variables. We propose a novel dedicated method to analyse this kind of hierarchical space, a random-forest-supervised HSIC-ANOVA, which ranks main effects and interactions natively on the tree while placing rarely and always active decisions on an equal footing. We show how, when applied to simulation outputs such as nitrogen leaching, soil organic carbon variation, and yield predictions, it can deliver an interpretable, decision-oriented reading.

articles.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.24006v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.

articles.title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.26787v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce LG-Bench, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

articles.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.30450v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.

articles.title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.30631v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Medical knowledge evolves, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate revisions into clinical recommendations remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change and 275 guideline lineages, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from its full incorporation. With updated guideline evidence explicitly provided, revision recognition exceeded full incorporation across 14 models, with a 20.1-percentage-point gap in the strongest model. For Qwen3-4B, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions, 80.2% were clinically correct, and 58.5% fully incorporated them, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point gap. Two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses yielded a 40.3-percentage-point gap in this enriched validation sample; 61 of 144 responses with incomplete incorporation were clinically incorrect. Prompting Qwen3-4B to prioritize revised evidence reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness without significantly improving full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of revised guidance as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability.

articles.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.32069v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.

articles.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.33465v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 17 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy differential equation benchmarks, LegoSR Agent nearly matches the recovery coverage of seven expert-tuned methods combined and exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 29.4 percentage points, with 51-61% shorter median wall-clock time.

articles.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.36116v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

articles.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.37161v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling supervised fine-tuning for working agents requires not only broad coverage of professional tasks, but also expert demonstrations that faithfully carry out professional workflows to completion. However, missing or inconsistent task information can disrupt expert demonstrations, weakening the resulting supervision. We introduce WorkFactory, a scalable task-construction framework that turns professional intents into executable task environments through hybrid intent sourcing, semantic workflow planning, and execution-based repair. Starting from these intents, WorkFactory constructs a Semantic Workflow Graph that explicitly represents information requirements, dependencies, and locations within the task environment. The graph guides the instantiation of task environments, while an adversarial execution-refinement loop exposes missing or inconsistent information and steers targeted repairs that preserve the original intent. Using WorkFactory, we construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and train the WorkPilot family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales on the resulting teacher trajectories. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B rising from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling experiments with up to 110k tasks further show that larger models benefit more from additional task data but exhibit diminishing returns at smaller data scales, while WorkPilot's long-horizon execution evolves from verbose trajectories toward more efficient task completion. Controlled component studies quantify the negative effects of task-environment defects on downstream performance and show how semantic workflow planning and execution-based repair yield downstream gains through improved task-environment quality. The subset of data are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.

articles.title: LiveSearch: Questions as Executable Verifier Code for a Live Benchmark of Professional-Source Financial Search Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.37166v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In finance, the answer that matters is usually the current one: prices, rates, and disclosures hold only as of a given day, so retrieving up-to-date facts is a core capability of a financial agent. Yet most financial benchmarks overlook timeliness. They fix each answer at annotation time, so the gold goes stale as markets move and, once leaked into training data, rewards recall rather than search and analysis. We introduce LiveSearch, a live benchmark that stores each question as executable verifier code: a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service, followed by a declarative extractor. The question is frozen, while its gold answer is determined by executing the program against professional financial data at evaluation time, and a daily job re-executes it with no human or language model in the loop. A memorized answer is thus likely outdated, and a model must reach the current one through tools and analysis. Construction is equally automatic: a language model only verbalizes programs enumerated from real tool responses and never chooses an answer. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy. Over three consecutive days, 70% of served questions change their gold value, and even under tolerance-aware matching, a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on a majority of questions within a single day. Per-question tracking uncovers dynamic shifts in correctness masked by aggregate accuracy.

articles.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.39070v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

articles.title: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.40959v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents achieve below 60% accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference, and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10% of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing SOTA model remains inconsistent on these capabilities. P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability, and safety of LLM-based personal agents.

articles.title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.41158v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

articles.title: Scaling Science: Toward a Chain Reaction of Discovery
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00580v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. Breaking this wall requires a paradigm shift in AI for Science: moving from passively mining questions out of existing datasets to actively generating and recombining experimental data around unresolved scientific questions. In a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates fresh evidence that stimulates further investigations. To enable these evidence-driven chain reactions, we propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint that connects shared scientific memory with distributed experimental loops. ESI preserves experimental records -- including negative and anomalous results -- in computable representations, allowing models to recombine evidence across domains into testable hypotheses. Rather than following fixed screening pipelines, the system jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, directing distributed laboratories to produce the exact evidence needed next. Their physical feedback revises both hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build this infrastructure for scaling science through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.

articles.title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00627v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large databases of paper-derived experimental materials data hide essential information on materials. Their analysis is demanding, large-scale and complex, making manual knowledge extraction very difficult. To address this challenge, we developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA) for automated, autonomous analysis of materials experimental big data and a specialized AI built on the obtained knowledge. MAA's nine role-specific AI agents, under predefined instructions and quality checks, autonomously perform data extraction, compositional feature generation, machine-learning modeling, feature-importance analysis and knowledge-base recording, iterating while inheriting previous knowledge. Delegating numerical processing to code makes large-scale data tractable; recording every choice and result enables later tracing to sources. In four thermoelectric-data experiments varying theme and cycle counts, the knowledge graph grew: knowledge clustered by theme and vocabulary was shared across themes. The specialized AI, searching and reading these records, answered materials questions citing sources. Retrospective verification also revealed errors, traced through the records to their sources.

articles.title: CHATDIFY: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.01563v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

articles.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.03412v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds together, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Reconstructed from real materials with 13 domain experts, its 11 projects span settings such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting. They comprise 150 subtasks, with 2-15 subsequent releases of new materials and client feedback per project. Later subtasks build on the agent's own earlier deliverables, so unresolved errors can carry into downstream work. Expert rubrics assess each subtask submission and the final delivery package. Across seven model-harness systems, the best scores 65.0/100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery; delivery also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

articles.title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.03698v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

articles.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.03721v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spectral response that shifts during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.

articles.title: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.04371v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.

articles.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.04483v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

articles.title: EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.06321v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Enzyme engineering usually optimises which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow; when the bottleneck is a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is hard to escape. We present EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop system for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights; the inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions; a cloud laboratory system is specified for closing the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback. The outer loop raised the mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin); of the two first places, only CD19 was produced by the outer loop itself. In ThermoMPNN self-improvement the inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849, and on TadA-Bench a Spearman correlation of 0.307 in 1.13 h. We examined the system's experimental decision-making in three enzyme systems. For the luciferase RLuc, 10 of the 32 nominated substitutions not pre-specified reached at least twice wild-type activity in a single round. For the cytidine deaminase A3A, a variant selected by a rule that caps loss of unmodified C raised 5mC conversion in the weaker CT context from 11.4% to 46.5% and reversed the substrate preference in both contexts. For the DNA polymerase KOD-E, 189 single-substitution variants defined a landscape on which different objective functions selected divergent next steps from the same parent; one assayed combination reached 31.1 times the parent on a modified substrate. By treating the organisation of research and the development of algorithms as separately scored objects of evolution, and linking a frozen decision record to a physical measurement, this work offers an evolutionary paradigm for moving beyond the blind spots of a fixed method and for autonomous enzyme engineering.

articles.title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.07482v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

articles.title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.07508v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI agents are expanding from personal assistance into professional services delivered to external clients on an individual's behalf. We define a personal external service agent as one authorized and managed on an ongoing basis by an individual. It uses that person's knowledge, experience, and professional methods to accept client work, deliver results, and provide follow-up support. Client feedback, professional reputation, and potential income may give individuals more direct incentives to keep developing and improving agents for external services than for personal assistance. Yet building a safe, reliable external service system independently remains difficult, even with AI-assisted programming. People without AI expertise need platforms that are easy to use and safe to operate, with support for creating, developing, and running their agents. We propose the DelegateEval evaluation framework and experimental design to assess these platforms and guide their development. The framework covers eight dimensions: ease of creation and management, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. A complete dataset, executable environment, and unified scoring protocol remain to be developed, and empirical validation across foundation models has yet to be conducted.

articles.title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.07520v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Resource closures, arrival delays, and processing-time extensions jointly alter station operations during disruptions. Uncertain reopening times further complicate decisions about holding trains and selecting alternative routes. We use observations of disruption-resolution stages to update conditional predictions of the remaining closure duration. A distributionally robust model accounts for errors in scenario probability estimates and jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. Logic-based Benders decomposition coordinates routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts exploit resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the solution order of resource relaxations. Together, these components form the GNN-LBBD algorithm. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min. This was 16.63% lower than tabu search and 20.06% lower than variable neighborhood search. Its mean total computation time was close to that of tabu search. On six representative instances, using stage observations reduced mean total completion delay by approximately 21.7%. Continued updating of reopening-time predictions allows route and entry-time adjustments during closures, reducing delays caused by waiting for reopening.

articles.title: PCBRouteAgent: How Close Are LLM Agents to Becoming PCB Routing Engineers?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08175v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.

articles.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08865v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

articles.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.09271v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

articles.title: KineCouple: Substrate-conditioned residual readout for enzyme kinetic prediction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.09377v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters can support enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling by complementing experimental characterization. Existing prediction methods often pool residue-level protein features before combining them with substrate features. Such substrate-independent pooling cannot adapt residue weighting to the substrate during aggregation, potentially diluting information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair. Since the contributions of individual residues to catalysis can depend on the substrate, substrate-conditioned aggregation offers a way to emphasize residue features relevant to the prediction. We introduce KineCouple, which uses substrate queries and residue-level keys and values in cross-attention, allowing the substrate to guide residue selection before aggregation. The model preserves the global protein representation and adds a gated correction defined as the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout. ProtT5 and MolT5 remain frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale. In pooled out-of-fold predictions on the CataPro benchmarks, KineCouple reduces kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330 and increases PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro. For Km, RMSE decreases from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC increases from 0.633 to 0.634. Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.

articles.title: Informed Posterior Sampling: More Efficient Online Learning with Few Offline Demonstrations in Average-Reward MDPs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2310.11531v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study efficient online reinforcement learning in the infinite horizon setting when there is an offline dataset to start with. We assume that the offline dataset is generated by an expert but with an unknown level of competence, i.e., it is not perfect and not necessarily using the optimal policy. We show that if the learning agent models the behavioral policy (parameterized by a competence parameter) used by the expert, it can do substantially better in terms of minimizing cumulative regret than if it does not do that. We establish an upper bound on regret of the exact informed PSRL (iPSRL) algorithm that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$. This requires a novel prior-dependent regret analysis of Bayesian online learning algorithms for the infinite horizon setting. We then propose the informed RLSVI (iRLSVI) algorithm to efficiently approximate the iPSRL algorithm. Empirical results show that small offline expert datasets are sufficient for iRLSVI to outperform online-only algorithms on hard exploration domains.

articles.title: Deep Tensor Network
articles.summary:
arXiv:2311.11091v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The Deep Tensor Network is a family of sequence operators built from contractions of queries, keys, and values. Tensor Attention mixes tokens through the Gram operators $Q(K^\top K)Q^\top$ and $K(Q^\top Q)K^\top$; Tensor Interaction mixes channels through operators derived from $C=Q^\top K$. Associativity lets us evaluate these products exactly without forming $n\times n$ token matrices. For query/key width $d$ and value width $d_v$, the Gram constructions use $O(d^2+dd_v)$ work and summary state per causal token, or $O(d^2)$ when $d_v=O(d)$. We derive prefix recurrences and distinguish trace, diagonal, and row normalization, including the conditions under which the weights are nonnegative and row-stochastic. The unmasked token operators are positive semidefinite with rank at most $d$, but their entries can be negative. We also give exact evaluations and costs for Hadamard and matrix-exponential variants.

articles.title: Generalized Influence Functions for Better Model Change Estimates
articles.summary:
arXiv:2312.05586v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Influence functions (IFs) approximate the effect of removing or reweighting training data on a trained model, but their linear approximation often lacks the accuracy required for reliable post hoc model editing. We identify two culprits and propose generalized influence functions (GIFs) and pseudo-LiSSA (p-LiSSA) to address each in turn. First, classical IFs update all parameters indiscriminately, leading to unnecessary updates to data-irrelevant parameters. GIFs instead restrict edits to a data-relevant subspace and leave the remaining parameters fixed. We theoretically show that GIFs achieve a tighter error bound than classical IFs when the parameter subset is properly selected, and that effective subspace selection requires avoiding low-curvature directions while retaining a sufficiently large component of the target gradient. Second, LiSSA iterations are destabilized by negative Hessian eigenvalues, which existing methods handle via $\ell_2$ damping, at the cost of a biased inverse-Hessian-vector product (iHVP) estimate. p-LiSSA eliminates this bias by solving the restricted inverse-Hessian problem without such damping. We further show that the presence of low-curvature directions slows p-LiSSA convergence, and that the data-relevant subspace selected by GIFs mitigates this. Across five image and text unlearning benchmarks, GIFs update only 10% of the parameters yet preserve accuracy up to 2.12 percentage points better than IF-based baselines, while improving unlearning performance by up to 2.73 percentage points. Moreover, p-LiSSA improves restricted iHVP estimation by reducing the residual by 9.6$\times$ over existing iHVP baselines, while using 19.8% less memory with comparable computation time. Code is available at https://github.com/hslyu/GIF.

articles.title: Learning temporal formulas from examples is hard
articles.summary:
arXiv:2312.16336v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the problem of learning linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas from examples, as a first step towards expressing a property separating positive and negative instances in a way that is comprehensible for humans. Given positive and negative words, the goal is to find a smallest formula satisfied by the positive words and not by the negative ones. We study the computational complexity of this problem for all fragments of negation-free LTL built from the operators F (eventually), G (globally), X (next), $\wedge$ (conjunction), and $\vee$ (disjunction), without the until operator. We show that the problem is in NP for all fragments, that it is in polynomial time for the fragments containing none of the pairs $\{X,\wedge\}$, $\{X,\vee\}$, $\{F,\wedge\}$ and $\{G,\vee\}$, and that it is NP-complete for all other fragments, already for alphabets with two or three letters. We also show that the fragment with only X and $\wedge$ has a polynomial time 3-approximation algorithm, but no polynomial time approximation scheme unless P = NP. These results motivate the search for efficient heuristics.

articles.title: CombAlign: Enhancing Model Expressiveness in Unsupervised Graph Alignment
articles.summary:
arXiv:2406.13216v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Unsupervised graph alignment finds the node correspondence between a pair of attributed graphs by only exploiting graph structure and node features. One category of recent studies first computes the node representation and then matches nodes with the largest embedding-based similarity, while the other category reduces the problem to optimal transport (OT) via Gromov-Wasserstein learning. However, it remains largely unexplored in the model expressiveness, as well as how theoretical expressivity impacts prediction accuracy. We investigate the model expressiveness from two aspects. First, we characterize the model's discriminative power in distinguishing matched and unmatched node pairs across two graphs. Second, we study the model's capability of guaranteeing node matching properties such as one-to-one matching and mutual alignment. Motivated by our theoretical analysis, we put forward a hybrid approach named CombAlign with stronger expressive power. Specifically, we enable cross-dimensional feature interaction for OT-based learning and propose an embedding-based method inspired by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. We also apply non-uniform marginals obtained from the embedding-based modules to OT as priors for more expressiveness. Based on that, we propose a traditional algorithm-based refinement, which combines our OT and embedding-based predictions using the ensemble learning strategy and reduces the problem to maximum weight matching. With carefully designed edge weights, we ensure these matching properties and further enhance prediction accuracy. By extensive experiments, we demonstrate a significant improvement of 14.5% in alignment accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches and confirm the soundness of our theoretical analysis.

articles.title: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
articles.summary:
arXiv:2410.04655v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings prevent mapping onto a reference shape, it predicts an 85-ms trajectory in under half a second, against about 5 minutes for finite elements, with a mean activation-time error of 1.73 ms. Accuracy depends on graph construction and is highest when the learned generator is integrated at its training time step.

articles.title: Embedded Decomposed Transformer for explainable multivariate time series forecasting
articles.summary:
arXiv:2412.12227v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Time series forecasting is an important problem with diverse real-world applications. This paper introduces the Embedded Decomposed Transformer (EDformer) for multivariate time series forecasting. EDformer decomposes the input signal into seasonal and trend components using two complementary strategies: time-domain Average Pooling (AP) based on moving-average smoothing and Frequency-Aware (FA) decomposition based on low-pass filtering in the Fourier domain. The reconstructed multivariate seasonal component is embedded across inverted dimensions, after which attention captures cross-variate correlations and a feed-forward network learns nonlinear representations for each variable. The trend component is forecast through projection and combined with the seasonal prediction to produce the final forecast. We evaluate both decomposition variants on several real-world datasets, showing that EDformer achieves competitive performance, while their relative effectiveness varies across datasets, experimental settings, and temporal characteristics. We further conduct an ablation study isolating the contribution of decomposition, inverted embedding, and the frequency cutoff ratio; a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over learning rate and batch size; and a statistical significance analysis using Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to substantiate the reported performance differences. Finally, model explainability techniques are explored to improve interpretability and provide insights into the features and time steps influencing the forecasting results.

articles.title: ViDE: Tuning-Free Video Coherence via Temporal Attention Reweighting and Prompt Blending
articles.summary:
arXiv:2412.17254v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Despite the substantial progress in long video generation, multi-prompt synthesis often encounters inconsistencies resulting from the training-inference gap caused by length extension techniques and coarse prompt interpolation. To overcome these issues, we propose the Video Diffusion with hidden states Editing (ViDE) framework, which consists of two key components. The first is the Time-frequency based Temporal Attention Reweighting (TiTAR) algorithm, which leverages the relationship between inconsistencies and diagonal elements of temporal attention.
